# Trivy Fundamentals — Security Scanning Fundamentals

## 1. Overview and Purpose

This section explains "Trivy Fundamentals — Security Scanning Fundamentals" within the navigation topic "Trivy Fundamentals" in the Trivy security scanning workflow. The subject belongs to the technical area of Trivy Fundamentals. Understand what the feature evaluates, why the security team uses it, which inputs it requires, and what result it produces. The purpose is to identify security risk early and provide evidence that developers and platform engineers can use during implementation and release validation.

## 2. Technical Explanation

Trivy is an open-source security scanner used to inspect software artifacts and supported configuration targets. Depending on the selected target and enabled scanners, it can identify vulnerabilities, exposed secrets, software components, and configuration risks. A scan must be interpreted in the context of its target, scanner selection, database state, and configuration. A successful command execution alone does not prove that every relevant security check was performed. Teams should record the Trivy version, scan target, scanner selection, and result so that findings can be reproduced and reviewed.

## 3. Section-Specific Engineering Focus

Technical implementation: explain the purpose of this subject, its inputs and outputs, the internal processing sequence, relevant Trivy behavior, practical DevOps usage, validation, and operational limitations.

The exact behavior must be verified against the installed Trivy version, selected target type, enabled scanners, and configuration. A scanner can only evaluate information it successfully discovers. Missing files, inaccessible artifacts, unsupported formats, stale databases, or incomplete permissions can reduce coverage. Always distinguish a clean result from a scan that did not complete successfully.

## 4. Practical DevOps Workflow

Start with a clearly identified source directory, configuration file, or immutable container image. Record the commit or image digest so the scan result can be connected to the artifact under review. Execute the relevant Trivy command, inspect the result, and evaluate findings using an approved security policy. Assign each actionable finding to an engineering owner. After a fix, rebuild or regenerate the artifact and repeat the scan rather than assuming that a source-code change automatically corrected the release artifact.

## 5. Validation and Troubleshooting

Verify the scanner version, target path, enabled scanner types, database availability, registry access, and output location. If the result is unexpected, compare the target that was scanned with the target that was intended. Inspect the finding identifier, affected resource or package, installed version, and available remediation details. For an execution error, resolve the underlying access, connectivity, configuration, or compatibility problem before treating the scan result as valid.

## 6. Production Best Practices

Use version-controlled scanner configuration, least-privilege credentials, protected report storage, immutable artifact references, and documented severity thresholds. Do not expose credentials in terminal output or pipeline logs. Avoid broad ignore rules. Document accepted risks with an owner and review date. Keep security reports associated with the relevant build and release so that incident responders can identify affected artifacts when new vulnerabilities are disclosed.

## 7. Learning Outcome

After completing "Trivy Fundamentals — Security Scanning Fundamentals", an engineer should be able to explain its purpose in "Trivy Fundamentals", identify the relevant Trivy workflow, execute or interpret the appropriate check, investigate an unexpected result, and verify the outcome using repeatable evidence. The engineer should also understand the limitations of the check and know when additional application, infrastructure, or runtime security validation is necessary.

It supports vulnerability investigations, license review, supply-chain visibility, and impact analysis when a package becomes unsafe. Trivy can generate supported SBOM formats for scanned targets. For example, trivy image --format cyclonedx --output sbom.json my-app:latest generates a CycloneDX output for an accessible image. Associate the SBOM with the exact image digest and release identifier. An SBOM is an inventory, not a guarantee that the listed software is secure.

Missing files, inaccessible artifacts, unsupported formats, stale databases, or incomplete permissions can reduce coverage. # Trivy Installation — Misconfiguration Detection

## 1. Overview and Purpose

This section explains "Trivy Installation — Misconfiguration Detection" within the navigation topic "Trivy Installation" in the Trivy security scanning workflow. The subject belongs to the technical area of Misconfiguration Scanning. Understand what the feature evaluates, why the security team uses it, which inputs it requires, and what result it produces. The purpose is to identify security risk early and provide evidence that developers and platform engineers can use during implementation and release validation.

## 2. Technical Explanation

Misconfiguration scanning evaluates supported infrastructure and application configuration files against security checks. Trivy config . can inspect supported files in the selected directory. Checks may identify insecure settings such as excessive permissions, unsafe exposure, or weak workload configuration. Findings should be reviewed with the affected resource, rule identifier, severity, and recommended remediation. The scanner evaluates the configuration it can discover; it does not automatically prove that deployed infrastructure has the same state or that runtime controls are effective.

## 3. Section-Specific Engineering Focus

Installation and setup: explain the required executable, supported environment, version verification, configuration, permissions, and network or database prerequisites.

The exact behavior must be verified against the installed Trivy version, selected target type, enabled scanners, and configuration. A scanner can only evaluate information it successfully discovers. Missing files, inaccessible artifacts, unsupported formats, stale databases, or incomplete permissions can reduce coverage. Always distinguish a clean result from a scan that did not complete successfully.

## 4. Practical DevOps Workflow

Start with a clearly identified source directory, configuration file, or immutable container image. Record the commit or image digest so the scan result can be connected to the artifact under review. Execute the relevant Trivy command, inspect the result, and evaluate findings using an approved security policy. Assign each actionable finding to an engineering owner. After a fix, rebuild or regenerate the artifact and repeat the scan rather than assuming that a source-code change automatically corrected the release artifact.

## 5. Validation and Troubleshooting

Verify the scanner version, target path, enabled scanner types, database availability, registry access, and output location. If the result is unexpected, compare the target that was scanned with the target that was intended. Inspect the finding identifier, affected resource or package, installed version, and available remediation details. For an execution error, resolve the underlying access, connectivity, configuration, or compatibility problem before treating the scan result as valid.

## 6. Production Best Practices

Use version-controlled scanner configuration, least-privilege credentials, protected report storage, immutable artifact references, and documented severity thresholds. Do not expose credentials in terminal output or pipeline logs. Avoid broad ignore rules. Document accepted risks with an owner and review date. Keep security reports associated with the relevant build and release so that incident responders can identify affected artifacts when new vulnerabilities are disclosed.

## 7. Learning Outcome

After completing "Trivy Installation — Misconfiguration Detection", an engineer should be able to explain its purpose in "Trivy Installation", identify the relevant Trivy workflow, execute or interpret the appropriate check, investigate an unexpected result, and verify the outcome using repeatable evidence. # Dependency Scanning — CI Pipeline Integration

## 1. Overview and Purpose

This section explains "Dependency Scanning — CI Pipeline Integration" within the navigation topic "Dependency Scanning" in the Trivy security scanning workflow. The subject belongs to the technical area of CI Pipeline Integration. Understand what the feature evaluates, why the security team uses it, which inputs it requires, and what result it produces. The purpose is to identify security risk early and provide evidence that developers and platform engineers can use during implementation and release validation.

## 2. Technical Explanation

CI pipeline integration runs security checks as part of the automated software delivery process. A practical sequence is source checkout, dependency validation, build, image scan, policy evaluation, artifact publication, and deployment. Trivy image --exit-code 1 --severity HIGH,CRITICAL my-app:latest can be used to make selected findings return a failing exit status. The pipeline must distinguish a security-policy failure from a scanner execution failure. Scan the final artifact, use immutable digests, protect report files, and make failure details available to the responsible engineering team.

## 3. Section-Specific Engineering Focus

Pipeline execution: explain where the scan belongs in the delivery workflow, how the target artifact is selected, how exit codes are evaluated, and how reports and failures are handled.

The exact behavior must be verified against the installed Trivy version, selected target type, enabled scanners, and configuration. A scanner can only evaluate information it successfully discovers. Missing files, inaccessible artifacts, unsupported formats, stale databases, or incomplete permissions can reduce coverage. Always distinguish a clean result from a scan that did not complete successfully.

## 4. Practical DevOps Workflow

Start with a clearly identified source directory, configuration file, or immutable container image. Record the commit or image digest so the scan result can be connected to the artifact under review. Execute the relevant Trivy command, inspect the result, and evaluate findings using an approved security policy. Assign each actionable finding to an engineering owner. After a fix, rebuild or regenerate the artifact and repeat the scan rather than assuming that a source-code change automatically corrected the release artifact.

## 5. Validation and Troubleshooting

Verify the scanner version, target path, enabled scanner types, database availability, registry access, and output location. If the result is unexpected, compare the target that was scanned with the target that was intended. Inspect the finding identifier, affected resource or package, installed version, and available remediation details. For an execution error, resolve the underlying access, connectivity, configuration, or compatibility problem before treating the scan result as valid.

## 6. Production Best Practices

Use version-controlled scanner configuration, least-privilege credentials, protected report storage, immutable artifact references, and documented severity thresholds. Do not expose credentials in terminal output or pipeline logs. Avoid broad ignore rules. Document accepted risks with an owner and review date. Keep security reports associated with the relevant build and release so that incident responders can identify affected artifacts when new vulnerabilities are disclosed.

## 7. Learning Outcome

After completing "Dependency Scanning — CI Pipeline Integration", an engineer should be able to explain its purpose in "Dependency Scanning", identify the relevant Trivy workflow, execute or interpret the appropriate check, investigate an unexpected result, and verify the outcome using repeatable evidence. The engineer should also understand the limitations of the check and know when additional application, infrastructure, or runtime security validation is necessary.

# Severity Classification — Secret Detection

## 1. Overview and Purpose

This section explains "Severity Classification — Secret Detection" within the navigation topic "Severity Classification" in the Trivy security scanning workflow. The subject belongs to the technical area of Secret Scanning. Understand what the feature evaluates, why the security team uses it, which inputs it requires, and what result it produces. The purpose is to identify security risk early and provide evidence that developers and platform engineers can use during implementation and release validation.

## 2. Technical Explanation

Secret scanning searches supported files and artifacts for values that may represent credentials or sensitive authentication material. Examples include API tokens, passwords, cloud keys, and private keys. A typical filesystem command is trivy fs --scanners secret . Detection results should be handled as confidential security data because reports may reveal sensitive locations or values. If a real credential is exposed, remove the exposure where appropriate, revoke or rotate the credential, investigate possible misuse, and move future secrets into an approved secrets manager.

## 3. Section-Specific Engineering Focus

Severity interpretation: explain how severity is represented, how teams should interpret the rating, why severity is not identical to exploitability, and how risk-based policy should be applied.

The exact behavior must be verified against the installed Trivy version, selected target type, enabled scanners, and configuration. A scanner can only evaluate information it successfully discovers. Missing files, inaccessible artifacts, unsupported formats, stale databases, or incomplete permissions can reduce coverage. Always distinguish a clean result from a scan that did not complete successfully.

## 4. Practical DevOps Workflow

Start with a clearly identified source directory, configuration file, or immutable container image. Record the commit or image digest so the scan result can be connected to the artifact under review. Execute the relevant Trivy command, inspect the result, and evaluate findings using an approved security policy. Assign each actionable finding to an engineering owner. After a fix, rebuild or regenerate the artifact and repeat the scan rather than assuming that a source-code change automatically corrected the release artifact.

Verify the scanner version, target path, enabled scanner types, database availability, registry access, and output location. If the result is unexpected, compare the target that was scanned with the target that was intended. # Secret Scanning — Security Scanning Fundamentals

## 1. Overview and Purpose

This section explains "Secret Scanning — Security Scanning Fundamentals" within the navigation topic "Secret Scanning" in the Trivy security scanning workflow. The subject belongs to the technical area of Secret Scanning. Understand what the feature evaluates, why the security team uses it, which inputs it requires, and what result it produces. The purpose is to identify security risk early and provide evidence that developers and platform engineers can use during implementation and release validation.

## 2. Technical Explanation

Secret scanning searches supported files and artifacts for values that may represent credentials or sensitive authentication material. Examples include API tokens, passwords, cloud keys, and private keys. A typical filesystem command is trivy fs --scanners secret . Detection results should be handled as confidential security data because reports may reveal sensitive locations or values. If a real credential is exposed, remove the exposure where appropriate, revoke or rotate the credential, investigate possible misuse, and move future secrets into an approved secrets manager.

## 3. Section-Specific Engineering Focus

Secret handling: explain the sensitive data involved, detection limitations, the risk of exposure, safe investigation, credential rotation, and prevention of future leaks.

The exact behavior must be verified against the installed Trivy version, selected target type, enabled scanners, and configuration. A scanner can only evaluate information it successfully discovers. Missing files, inaccessible artifacts, unsupported formats, stale databases, or incomplete permissions can reduce coverage. Always distinguish a clean result from a scan that did not complete successfully.

## 4. Practical DevOps Workflow

Start with a clearly identified source directory, configuration file, or immutable container image. Record the commit or image digest so the scan result can be connected to the artifact under review. Execute the relevant Trivy command, inspect the result, and evaluate findings using an approved security policy. Assign each actionable finding to an engineering owner. After a fix, rebuild or regenerate the artifact and repeat the scan rather than assuming that a source-code change automatically corrected the release artifact.

## 5. Validation and Troubleshooting

Verify the scanner version, target path, enabled scanner types, database availability, registry access, and output location. If the result is unexpected, compare the target that was scanned with the target that was intended. Inspect the finding identifier, affected resource or package, installed version, and available remediation details. For an execution error, resolve the underlying access, connectivity, configuration, or compatibility problem before treating the scan result as valid.

## 6. Production Best Practices

Use version-controlled scanner configuration, least-privilege credentials, protected report storage, immutable artifact references, and documented severity thresholds. Do not expose credentials in terminal output or pipeline logs. Avoid broad ignore rules. Document accepted risks with an owner and review date. Keep security reports associated with the relevant build and release so that incident responders can identify affected artifacts when new vulnerabilities are disclosed.

## 7. Learning Outcome

After completing "Secret Scanning — Security Scanning Fundamentals", an engineer should be able to explain its purpose in "Secret Scanning", identify the relevant Trivy workflow, execute or interpret the appropriate check, investigate an unexpected result, and verify the outcome using repeatable evidence. The engineer should also understand the limitations of the check and know when additional application, infrastructure, or runtime security validation is necessary.

Verify the scanner version, target path, enabled scanner types, database availability, registry access, and output location. # Ignore Policies — Secret Detection

## 1. Overview and Purpose

This section explains "Ignore Policies — Secret Detection" within the navigation topic "Ignore Policies" in the Trivy security scanning workflow. The subject belongs to the technical area of Secret Scanning. Understand what the feature evaluates, why the security team uses it, which inputs it requires, and what result it produces. The purpose is to identify security risk early and provide evidence that developers and platform engineers can use during implementation and release validation.

## 2. Technical Explanation

Secret scanning searches supported files and artifacts for values that may represent credentials or sensitive authentication material. Examples include API tokens, passwords, cloud keys, and private keys. A typical filesystem command is trivy fs --scanners secret . Detection results should be handled as confidential security data because reports may reveal sensitive locations or values. If a real credential is exposed, remove the exposure where appropriate, revoke or rotate the credential, investigate possible misuse, and move future secrets into an approved secrets manager.

## 3. Section-Specific Engineering Focus

Policy exceptions: explain the scope of an exception, how it affects findings, approval and ownership requirements, expiration or review, and how to avoid hiding unrelated security risks.

The exact behavior must be verified against the installed Trivy version, selected target type, enabled scanners, and configuration. A scanner can only evaluate information it successfully discovers. Missing files, inaccessible artifacts, unsupported formats, stale databases, or incomplete permissions can reduce coverage. Always distinguish a clean result from a scan that did not complete successfully.

Start with a clearly identified source directory, configuration file, or immutable container image. Record the commit or image digest so the scan result can be connected to the artifact under review. # CI Pipeline Integration — Production Security Workflow

## 1. Overview and Purpose

This section explains "CI Pipeline Integration — Production Security Workflow" within the navigation topic "CI Pipeline Integration" in the Trivy security scanning workflow. The subject belongs to the technical area of Severity Classification. Understand what the feature evaluates, why the security team uses it, which inputs it requires, and what result it produces. The purpose is to identify security risk early and provide evidence that developers and platform engineers can use during implementation and release validation.

## 2. Technical Explanation

Severity classification communicates the assessed seriousness of a security finding. Trivy reports severity values such as UNKNOWN, LOW, MEDIUM, HIGH, and CRITICAL where supported by the underlying vulnerability information. Severity is an important prioritization signal, but it is not a complete measure of business risk. Exploitability, exposure, affected runtime paths, compensating controls, and asset importance also matter. A production policy should define thresholds, ownership, escalation, and exception approval rather than treating every finding with the same operational response.

## 3. Section-Specific Engineering Focus

Severity interpretation: explain how severity is represented, how teams should interpret the rating, why severity is not identical to exploitability, and how risk-based policy should be applied.

The exact behavior must be verified against the installed Trivy version, selected target type, enabled scanners, and configuration. A scanner can only evaluate information it successfully discovers. Missing files, inaccessible artifacts, unsupported formats, stale databases, or incomplete permissions can reduce coverage. Always distinguish a clean result from a scan that did not complete successfully.

## 4. Practical DevOps Workflow

Start with a clearly identified source directory, configuration file, or immutable container image. Record the commit or image digest so the scan result can be connected to the artifact under review. Execute the relevant Trivy command, inspect the result, and evaluate findings using an approved security policy. Assign each actionable finding to an engineering owner. After a fix, rebuild or regenerate the artifact and repeat the scan rather than assuming that a source-code change automatically corrected the release artifact.

## 5. Validation and Troubleshooting

Verify the scanner version, target path, enabled scanner types, database availability, registry access, and output location. If the result is unexpected, compare the target that was scanned with the target that was intended. Inspect the finding identifier, affected resource or package, installed version, and available remediation details. For an execution error, resolve the underlying access, connectivity, configuration, or compatibility problem before treating the scan result as valid.

## 6. Production Best Practices

Use version-controlled scanner configuration, least-privilege credentials, protected report storage, immutable artifact references, and documented severity thresholds. Do not expose credentials in terminal output or pipeline logs. Avoid broad ignore rules. Document accepted risks with an owner and review date. Keep security reports associated with the relevant build and release so that incident responders can identify affected artifacts when new vulnerabilities are disclosed.

## 7. Learning Outcome

After completing "CI Pipeline Integration — Production Security Workflow", an engineer should be able to explain its purpose in "CI Pipeline Integration", identify the relevant Trivy workflow, execute or interpret the appropriate check, investigate an unexpected result, and verify the outcome using repeatable evidence. The subject belongs to the technical area of Misconfiguration Scanning. Understand what the feature evaluates, why the security team uses it, which inputs it requires, and what result it produces. The purpose is to identify security risk early and provide evidence that developers and platform engineers can use during implementation and release validation.

## 2. Technical Explanation

Misconfiguration scanning evaluates supported infrastructure and application configuration files against security checks. Trivy config . can inspect supported files in the selected directory. Checks may identify insecure settings such as excessive permissions, unsafe exposure, or weak workload configuration. Findings should be reviewed with the affected resource, rule identifier, severity, and recommended remediation. The scanner evaluates the configuration it can discover; it does not automatically prove that deployed infrastructure has the same state or that runtime controls are effective.

## 3. Section-Specific Engineering Focus

Remediation: explain how to identify the affected component, select a supported fixed version, evaluate compatibility, test the change, rebuild the artifact, and verify the result with a fresh scan.

The exact behavior must be verified against the installed Trivy version, selected target type, enabled scanners, and configuration. A scanner can only evaluate information it successfully discovers. Missing files, inaccessible artifacts, unsupported formats, stale databases, or incomplete permissions can reduce coverage. Always distinguish a clean result from a scan that did not complete successfully.

## 4. Practical DevOps Workflow

Start with a clearly identified source directory, configuration file, or immutable container image. Record the commit or image digest so the scan result can be connected to the artifact under review. Execute the relevant Trivy command, inspect the result, and evaluate findings using an approved security policy. Assign each actionable finding to an engineering owner. After a fix, rebuild or regenerate the artifact and repeat the scan rather than assuming that a source-code change automatically corrected the release artifact.

## 5. Validation and Troubleshooting

Verify the scanner version, target path, enabled scanner types, database availability, registry access, and output location. If the result is unexpected, compare the target that was scanned with the target that was intended. Inspect the finding identifier, affected resource or package, installed version, and available remediation details. For an execution error, resolve the underlying access, connectivity, configuration, or compatibility problem before treating the scan result as valid.

## 6. Production Best Practices

Use version-controlled scanner configuration, least-privilege credentials, protected report storage, immutable artifact references, and documented severity thresholds. Do not expose credentials in terminal output or pipeline logs. Avoid broad ignore rules. Document accepted risks with an owner and review date. Keep security reports associated with the relevant build and release so that incident responders can identify affected artifacts when new vulnerabilities are disclosed.

After completing "Vulnerability Remediation — Misconfiguration Detection", an engineer should be able to explain its purpose in "Vulnerability Remediation", identify the relevant Trivy workflow, execute or interpret the appropriate check, investigate an unexpected result, and verify the outcome using repeatable evidence. # Troubleshooting — Security Scanning Fundamentals — Troubleshooting [stage-7-topic-15-section-17]

## 1. Overview and Purpose

This section explains "Troubleshooting — Security Scanning Fundamentals — Troubleshooting [stage-7-topic-15-section-17]" within the navigation topic "Troubleshooting" in the Trivy security scanning workflow. The subject belongs to the technical area of Troubleshooting. Understand what the feature evaluates, why the security team uses it, which inputs it requires, and what result it produces. The purpose is to identify security risk early and provide evidence that developers and platform engineers can use during implementation and release validation.

## 2. Technical Explanation

Trivy troubleshooting begins by separating scanner execution problems from actual security findings. Common causes include an incorrect target path, unsupported file formats, registry authentication failures, network or proxy problems, unavailable vulnerability databases, permission errors, and invalid command options. Collect the command, scanner version, target identity, exit status, and relevant error output without exposing secrets. Verify the target independently, check database and registry connectivity, and repeat the scan after correcting the cause. A failed or incomplete scan must never be interpreted as a clean security result.

## 3. Section-Specific Engineering Focus

Troubleshooting: explain the symptoms, likely technical causes, evidence to collect, diagnostic commands, safe corrective actions, and the validation required before closing the issue.

The exact behavior must be verified against the installed Trivy version, selected target type, enabled scanners, and configuration. A scanner can only evaluate information it successfully discovers. Missing files, inaccessible artifacts, unsupported formats, stale databases, or incomplete permissions can reduce coverage. Always distinguish a clean result from a scan that did not complete successfully.

## 4. Practical DevOps Workflow

Start with a clearly identified source directory, configuration file, or immutable container image. Record the commit or image digest so the scan result can be connected to the artifact under review. Execute the relevant Trivy command, inspect the result, and evaluate findings using an approved security policy. Assign each actionable finding to an engineering owner. After a fix, rebuild or regenerate the artifact and repeat the scan rather than assuming that a source-code change automatically corrected the release artifact.

## 5. Validation and Troubleshooting

Verify the scanner version, target path, enabled scanner types, database availability, registry access, and output location. If the result is unexpected, compare the target that was scanned with the target that was intended. Inspect the finding identifier, affected resource or package, installed version, and available remediation details. For an execution error, resolve the underlying access, connectivity, configuration, or compatibility problem before treating the scan result as valid.

## 6. Production Best Practices

Use version-controlled scanner configuration, least-privilege credentials, protected report storage, immutable artifact references, and documented severity thresholds. Do not expose credentials in terminal output or pipeline logs. Avoid broad ignore rules. Document accepted risks with an owner and review date. Keep security reports associated with the relevant build and release so that incident responders can identify affected artifacts when new vulnerabilities are disclosed.

## 7. Learning Outcome

After completing "Troubleshooting — Security Scanning Fundamentals — Troubleshooting [stage-7-topic-15-section-17]", an engineer should be able to explain its purpose in "Troubleshooting", identify the relevant Trivy workflow, execute or interpret the appropriate check, investigate an unexpected result, and verify the outcome using repeatable evidence. The engineer should also understand the limitations of the check and know when additional application, infrastructure, or runtime security validation is necessary.

# Production Hands-on Lab — Secret Detection

## 1. Overview and Purpose

This section explains "Production Hands-on Lab — Secret Detection" within the navigation topic "Production Hands-on Lab" in the Trivy security scanning workflow. The subject belongs to the technical area of Secret Scanning. Understand what the feature evaluates, why the security team uses it, which inputs it requires, and what result it produces. The purpose is to identify security risk early and provide evidence that developers and platform engineers can use during implementation and release validation.

## 2. Technical Explanation

Secret scanning searches supported files and artifacts for values that may represent credentials or sensitive authentication material. Examples include API tokens, passwords, cloud keys, and private keys. A typical filesystem command is trivy fs --scanners secret . Detection results should be handled as confidential security data because reports may reveal sensitive locations or values.
